html:
The World Bank is an international bank, owned by the governments of most countries, that lends money to poorer countries for development. It was set up at the Bretton Woods conference in 1944, together with the International Monetary Fund, and is based in Washington.

Its first loans, from 1947, helped rebuild Europe after the Second World War. Soon it turned to the newly independent countries of Asia, Africa and Latin America, lending for dams, power lines, roads and farming. Projects such as Ghana's Akosombo Dam were typical. It also brokered deals: India and Pakistan signed the Indus Waters Treaty in 1960 after nine years of talks it ran.

From 1960 a branch for the poorest countries made loans on very easy terms, and under Robert McNamara in the 1970s the bank put the fight against poverty at its centre. In the 1980s and 1990s it tied loans to "structural adjustment", demanding cuts to state spending and open markets. Critics said this hurt the poor.

Later it backed newer ideas, such as cash transfers to poor families on the model of Brazil's Bolsa Família, solar power at Noor Ouarzazate and the dam that revived the North Aral fishery. It can also walk away: in 2012 it cancelled its loan for Bangladesh's Padma Bridge over claims of corruption.
